utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't even know that Srebrenica would fall on that day. I was at Jaglici. I hadn't taken any documents with me before that. And when I set out, I didn't even know -- I didn't go back to Srebrenica in order to get the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it standard practice in your division, when a unit went out to carry out an assignment, that people wouldn't have their or take their IDs with them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no such practice, but I know that most men did not have IDs because there was no use for it. Who was going to check for IDs? You don't expect that they would do it on the border. They would just go out to the front-line to defend it, so they didn't need their IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, on page 97 of the transcript, you said that at the moment when you were surrendering, you had actually tossed away the hand-grenades that you had with you and the weapon that you had with you. You said that you had actually dropped them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the hand-grenades, actually, I dropped them. I didn't throw them away or anything. They just got -- they were hooked on to my belt, and then as I was actually crawling and trying to get across, they got unhooked, and that's how they fell out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, tell me, when was that? Was that on the day when you set out to break through, or where was it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't a breakthrough; it was an ambush at Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what day this was on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 12th of July, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the column -- did the column actually form then, and did the column set out from Sandici? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which column you're referring to. Later on, there were quite a few columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say to the OTP in your statement that the column was formed in Sandici, and did you say that Commander Becirovic addressed you, that he spoke to the -- addressed the column through a bullhorn? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The column was formed in Kamenica. A group of us who were there, we just formed a column in order to pull out the wounded, so that when we set out, we ran into ambush, and they opened fire on us again, and we dispersed. The wounded remained in the field there, so -- and that's it. There was no other column or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the commander address the column in Susnjari? Because that's what you said in your statement -- in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that about the bullhorn or megaphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, do you consider yourself to be armed if you had with you hand-grenades? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that, for self-defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now show the witness document 1D0017, page 2 in the Serbian language and page 3 in English. This is a statement provided by this witness to the BH MUP in Tuzla on the 22nd of July, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the last sentence -- the last line on page 2 of the B/C/S version. At one point, one of the prisoners said that the Chetnik leader, Radovan Karadzic, made an appearance -- showed up for a moment at the window of the gymnasium: "I did not see him personally, but many of the people in the gym confirmed that." My question: Witness, tell us, please, why did you state this in your statement when you were not an eye-witness and where you actually just conveyed something that somebody else had said or seen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe there was an error made when it was written down. Karadzic did not show up at the window, but at the door of the gym, and maybe there was -- maybe this was just written down in error as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Could you tell us, please, at what time and on what day did you see Radovan Karadzic at the door? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact time because I didn't have a watch, and that was on the 14th, the same day that I was taken to the execution site where I was shot at. I didn't have a watch, so I couldn't tell you what time it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see the first page of this document, the same page -- the same page in the English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement, in English and in Serbian, you say: "The aggression on Srebrenica, when it started I was in the village of Lehovici, precisely on 6 July 1995, at the hands of SDS members and the Yugoslav Army." Do you stand by what you said then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I want to say that I speak Bosnian and not Serbian. And, yes, I did -- I do stand by what I said then. We were attacked by both the SDS, the Serbian SDS, and the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, could you please tell this Trial Chamber how it was. What does that mean, you were attacked by the SDS? Is that something that you knew, yourself, or that you heard from someone?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the SDS was in power then, and they were the one who started this war, so who else could it have been?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness now be shown his statement to this Tribunal. That's document 1D108 [as interpreted]. I'd like page 4 to be shown to the witness, and in English that's page 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The number is 1D18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, can you see the document before you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mention here -- you state that you were captured. That's in the third paragraph in the B/C/S translation. You were captured by JNA soldiers, and there was a Bosnian Serb Chetnik with them. Is that what you stated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was captured by Serb soldiers. Serbs, they captured me. And when we were held in the warehouse, then an officer who had a star came; he addressed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, what did this officer tell you at the warehouse? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked us where our rifles were, where we had left them, and to go and get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What led you to the conclusion that this was a JNA officer, as you said, although the JNA did not exist anymore at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people claim that to this day there is JNA. What do you mean, it didn't exist? I mean, these people were accused of the operation against Sarajevo. But I recognised him because he spoke in the Serbian accent from Serbia, which differs from the Bosnian accent, and also I could see that he had rank insignia on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you say what you saw? What type of insignia did you see on his shoulder patch? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just told you, I couldn't really see clearly what it was, but I did see a shoulder patch. I did not dare get up and stare at him. I was sitting, and he was standing in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell me if he was wearing a camouflage uniform or some other kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the shirt was the shirt that was used by the real Yugoslav Army. I know because I served in the army for four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So he had an old shirt of the JNA, whereas the JNA ceased to exist and the Army of Yugoslavia was formed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had the old uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, other than the fact that he spoke in the Serbian accent and the uniform -- the shirt that he wore, was there anything else that led you to the conclusion that he was a JNA member?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the soldiers addressed him and said that he didn't know anything about what was to happen to us, that his job was just to guard us, to capture us. That was their task. They had come there only to capture us. And he, too, spoke in the Serbian dialect. He didn't speak Bosnian, and I know that because I worked for a while in Serbia. So when he said that their task was to capture them and send them -- capture us and send us to Bratunac, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me whether there was still some specimens of old uniforms in Srebrenica that were used by the former JNA and issued by them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What did the TO in Srebrenica wear before the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO before the war? I don't know who was in the TO, I don't know what the TO was, I don't know what their uniforms were like. Well, I know the blue uniforms that they wore in the factories. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you a military conscript before the war?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I did not complete the military term of duty. I was returned after four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that all military conscripts, regardless of whether they were fit for duty or not, received a rucksack with equipment and a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I never received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone in Srebrenica was issued with a rucksack and a uniform of the former JNA that was kept in the TO warehouses?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say that I went around all the flats to look at what -- who had what. I don't know where this TO was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I think you responded to the question as far as you're able to, and the Trial Chamber knows they have the insignia of all the former militaries in the former Yugoslavia in their material. I have it here, but we're not going to waste any more time on that. We have that, the Prosecutor has that, everybody has that. Witness, can you please just tell me this: Is it possible, perhaps, that the Serbian soldiers kept the uniforms they were issued by the JNA, or did they throw it out after the JNA withdrew from Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know if they threw them away or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will have our second break now. We adjourn, and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00, and then you can continue with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may just ask one question for our witness planning purposes. If we could get some estimate, please, from the Defence about how much more cross, because we've had a witness who's been sitting in the witness room for some time, and if we're going to continue through the rest of the day, we'd just as soon liberate the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was prepared to raise the question at the end of today's sitting, because we didn't get any indication from the Defence about the length of the cross-examination. And for planning purposes for parties and for the Chamber, it would be very helpful if the accused, the Defence, would comply with our order of the 24th of February in this respect. Could you give an estimation -- indication if you will continue the whole day and perhaps even next week with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we will be able to finish with this witness today. I have a total of 117 questions. Last time, at the end of the hearing, I said that I did not manage to put all my questions, and how many questions I had left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, in this case, we can't be of the opinion that the next witness could be called today. That is for the Prosecution. Thank you. We adjourn and resume five minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, during the last session you -- we have seen two statements on the screen, but you were not tendering them. Perhaps it was an omission, but perhaps you don't want to have them tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do not want to ask for anything other than the things that I've already asked to be tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then please carry on with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, can you briefly reply if you know that in 1993, the government of Alija Izetbegovic charged Yugoslavia before the International Court of Justice and not against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Since you don't know, we're not going to be dealing with that question anymore. During your testimony, did you speak about who attacked Srebrenica? You spoke about the SDS and Yugoslavia attacking Srebrenica. Was anything like that suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that without anybody's prompting. I don't know if that was correctly written or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it also suggested to you to say in your statement that you also saw Mladic and Karadzic or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say I saw Karadzic. I did see Mladic in the sports hall, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you provided your statement to the Tribunal, were you warned that the JNA does not exist anymore and that the military operation in 1995 was not carried out by the Yugoslav People's Army or the Army of Yugoslavia, but the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. Perhaps it was written like that by mistake. I didn't say that. What's in the statement about the police, what I said about the Konjevic Polje and them being there, which I could tell by the way they spoke and by their ranks, this is something that I assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. You assumed that, but you are not sure. Thank you, thank you. You said, and the Prosecutor also said that in the summary of your testimony, that you arrived in Nezuk on the 21st of July, 1995. My question is: Would you personally believe the testimony of two witnesses who disagree about one very important thing, about the events that, by their nature, cannot be forgotten? The witness who testified before you, I will not tell his name because he was a protected witness, said that you came to Nezuk on the 19th of July, and you said the 21st of July. And we saw here, on this photograph, that the column arrived on the 16th, so what is the accurate fact here, then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of that can be shown. On the 21st, in the morning, I came to Nezuk by myself, and I was found by our soldiers, the person who survived together with me and who --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please can you not speak the names out. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have to say the names of people who were travelling with me. They were going with me, but we came to this bunker. They had left already on the 20th. I was going in the opposite side, so on the 21st, I -- they found me in a creek. They were, on the 20th, going along the road, and they said, Whoever was there, the Chetniks, our people, whoever, we cannot go further. So they went along the road, and they immediately encountered our barricade that was on the road. This was on the 20th, at night. They said that I had left, that I had gone in the opposite direction, but they were expecting me to come alone on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Can the witness be shown 1D032. This is a document of the Main Staff of the B and H Army, of the 17th of February, 1995, which was sent urgently to the Command of the 2nd Corps, the Command of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica, and the Command of the 1st Zepa Brigade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the number of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And again with the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is 1D32. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can see that the document is here. I'm being told so by my legal advisor. As a member of the B and H Army in Srebrenica, the witness could respond to some of my questions in relation to the contents of this document. And I can see that this document can also be used in order to get some answers from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 832, line 21 to 23, the document says that there were no preparations before the operation to capture Srebrenica began. He says, I quote: "People were working in the fields, and they were busy with their homes. They were working in the fields, and their only duty was, for example, like it was in my case, to patrol in the area." In this document -- I didn't ask for this document to be shown. 1D32, it says, I quote: "According to our information --" We are talking about paragraph 2: "We estimate that the aggressor will start offensive combat operations with the aim of completely over-powering the Milici-Podravanje road and then attempt to capture the territory of the demilitarised zones." I don't need to read further. I just want to read what is relevant for this question that I am about to put to the witness, which says -- the document says, regarding the development of the situation about the Zepa and Srebrenica -- it's actually on page 1 of the B/C/S and the Serbian. I'm don't want to read the whole document. I'm going to only quote three segments from the order. Thank you. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm reading the document 1D32, just a part of the order: "I order," first of all, "place the OG units on full combat readiness, securing entirely readiness for a successful reaction to actions by the aggressor."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness [as interpreted] please be asked to tell the interpreters where he's reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "3. The forces that you are placing in full combat readiness and other measures that you undertake should be taken in strict secrecy in order to prevent the arguments of the aggressor in relation to violation of agreements on the demilitarised zone, protected zone." All of this says in the English -- is said in the English on page 2. My legal advisor is telling me that this is not being shown correctly in the English. Can you please show us page 2 in the English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, we saw in your testimony in the Popovic case that you referred to mobilisation for purposes of the defence of Srebrenica; is that correct? Was there a mobilisation carried out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We also saw that you were armed and that while surrendering, you represented yourself as a civilian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a rifle. I did not introduce myself as a civilian. I mean, I didn't say anything. It was up to whoever was looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the B and H Army members in Srebrenica wear clothing without any recognisable and visible insignia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any insignia at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statements and testimony here -- actually, in your testimony here today and yesterday before the Trial Chamber, did you say that there was no military preparation carried out in Srebrenica for activities and support to Sarajevo? Yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demobilisation [as interpreted] was carried out when there was an attack on Srebrenica. I don't know for any other mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When I asked you a little bit earlier, 20 minutes ago, whether your unit participated in those preparations pursuant to that order by Becirovic, you said that you hadn't -- you didn't know anything about that and that they did not. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. But when there was the attack on Srebrenica, then we were all mobilised to hold the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it your duty to maintain the secrecy of confidential military orders and plans that were issued for purposes of the preparation for combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive anything secret, nor was it my duty to maintain the secrecy of such documents, and I don't know anything about any operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please give us your comments on this order? For example, paragraph 3, I'm repeating it in case you forgot: "Bringing units to full combat readiness and other measures must be taken under strict secrecy in order to eliminate any grounds on the aggressor's part for violations of the agreement on the demilitarised zone (protected zone)." Thank you. Can you please comment what was being asked here in this particular order by the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from your forces and from your operations group.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert to be able to answer that question. This is the first time that I see this document, and I know nothing about these things, and I don't know how to comment on it. I was never entrusted any secrets to keep, nor do I know about any secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, please, did you wear civilian clothes because there were no uniforms or because this zone enjoyed the status of a protected area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is -- the reason is that we didn't have uniforms. You showed me a paper stating that 600 uniforms were sent for a division. Now, you know the number of men in a division. You could not really dress 10.000 men in 600 uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does demilitarisation also -- did it also imply that all conscripts should be demilitarised -- demobilised?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that the reason why most of them were in civilian clothes, and since they did not hand over their uniforms to UNPROFOR, what happened to those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when UNPROFOR first arrived, we didn't even have six uniforms. They only came later by helicopter, as you said, in 1995 or so. As for UNPROFOR, it had arrived there in 1993, and there weren't any uniforms then. As for the uniforms you were mentioning, they were probably distributed to some other units. I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you, but I was just quoting an order that was sent by Rasim Delic via Hajrulahovic to Izetbegovic. Thank you. Could we now please see 1D38, a "New York Times" article of 30th May 1996 which is entitled "A Witness to a War Crime May Refuse to Testify." While we are waiting for the document to come up, I would like to tender the document that I just showed to the witness into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D16, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do we have the document before us? We will only use the first and fifth paragraph. This takes us in the English language, and I will read the translation into Serbian to the witness. I quote -- or, rather, I'm translating: "A key witness in the war crimes case against the Bosnian Serb military commander said Wednesday that because he had been given no protection by the International War Crimes Tribunal or the Bosnian government, he might refuse to testify out of fear that he or a member of his family would be killed by Serbian assassins."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question -- and I apologise, there was another sentence here which said: "I can't believe that they can't find a place for me and my family that is safe." And that's the end of the quotation. Witness, is this something that you stated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you don't remember, could you tell us this: You testified in several cases before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because of that, were you subject to any attacks, and who was it that actually threatened your security, and which Serbian assassins are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were never any attacks against me. And as for what is said here, I don't really recall. And I have no idea how the interpreter or translator translated it, but I don't remember this, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you don't remember saying that you were afraid of Serbian assassins, and there were no threats issued to you, and you weren't in any way in danger; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were no threats, but, yes, I was afraid; not too frightened, but it's normal for a person to be frightened. That's the reason why I don't really go to Republika Srpska, I don't go about Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see document 1D25. This is an interview with this witness on the 4th of January, 1998, and also an interview with the witness on the 18th of October, 1998. Do we have it before us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this report, it says, and I quote: "Mevludin Oric confirmed that he is willing to come to The Hague to testify. He had told a newspaper that he would not, but that was only because he was irritated by the authorities who had not given him proper support. He is fully aware of the importance of his testimony." My question is this: Is what I've just quoted correct? And I've quoted an information report -- an interview conducted with you by an OTP investigator. And is what was published in "The New York Times" correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about the article in "The New York Times," I don't know about that. About for what I said here, that I was irritated by my own government, that's true, because they never offered any kind of assistance ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. So you did not expect to be a protected witness here; you were actually referring to financial support? Have I understood what you just said properly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did say that I would testify as a public witness. And as for the authorities and what I stated there, that had to do with financial assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you consider -- do you feel that the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina owes you to reimburse you financially for your testimony -- testifying here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think they should, on behalf of all those people who did not survive, and I have, and they should provide some kind of support to me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there any pressure by the OTP on you to testify before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the statement that I quoted a moment earlier, when you said that you couldn't believe that neither the Tribunal or the BH government could provide a safe place for you, were you referring to a place where you would relocate with your family? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time when I stated that, I had great financial difficulties, but many things have changed since then, and it is now a bit better. But at the time in 1998, it wasn't good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell me, please, did you ever receive any kind of remuneration or financial assistance for testifying before this Tribunal? And if so, what kind of -- what amount was that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, there was no financial support. I just got per diem for coming here. And as for the per diem, that was what I got or get, and I would get the same thing if I were to work for this organisation. So I -- I get the same amount that I would get for my work in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Tribunal actually remunerate you, or how does that work?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But when I come here to The Hague, I get the per diems. As for my government, they don't provide for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And during the proofing session before you appeared as a witness for the first time before this Tribunal, did you get any remuneration from the BH government or any other international organisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I had, but, no, nobody would give me anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, for your answers, and I have no further questions in this cross-examination. I thank you, and I thank everyone else for their support today and for their understanding. Thank you, Mr. President. And I would like to tender this statement into evidence, the interview -- the newspaper interview, and the information report. Or, rather, this information report has already been entered into evidence. In other words, 1D32 and 1D25, I tender both of these into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1D32 is already an exhibit, we have received it already. The article from the "The New York Times," we didn't see any translation on the screen. I don't know if there is any in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will receive the information report of the 11th of October, 1998, which we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid misunderstandings, we saw "The New York Times" article on the screen in English. Do you tender that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, if you so decide, I would like to tender that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there any translation into B/C/S? Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this point in time, we do not have a translation. We only have the portion that we quoted. We do not have a translation into B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That article will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D18, marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, perhaps I missed something, but I would like to take you back to page 65 of today's transcript, line 10 to 12, and I would -- no, sorry, it was the wrong quotation. Just a moment. On page 61, lines 3 to 4, we have on the record in the transcript the following sentence, I quote: "The demobilisation was carried out when there was an attack on Srebrenica. I don't know for any other mobilisation." Are you talking about demobilisation or mobilisation? Could you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was mobilisation when the attack on Srebrenica began, so on that very first day people were mobilised, and they were supposed to be deployed along the front-line from which the UNPROFOR troops had withdrawn. And as for the other mobilisations that the accused mentioned, I don't know anything about that, about the sabotage and special units being mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is clear now. Mr. Oric, the Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance today and the last day of the hearing last week. Thank you very much -- or the beginning of this week. Thank you very much that you could make it to come here again to The Hague. You are free now to return to your normal activities, and we are -- all of us would like to thank you. All the best, thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, unexpectedly we are at the end of this evidence now, a little bit earlier than expected. I suppose you have sent back the next witness for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, we have to adjourn now and resume on Monday, I think in the afternoon, if I'm not mistaken. Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber would be grateful if you could provide us with information about the length of anticipated cross-examination of the next witnesses which are scheduled for next week and especially for the witnesses scheduled for April. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume on Monday.
